segments.text: Indexes: how the database finds rows fast.
Think of a phone book. To find Ruiz, you don't read every page. The names are sorted, so you jump straight to R.
An index does the same for a table: a separate, sorted structure that points to the rows.
Here is the customer table of the shop: fifty thousand rows. We want the customer with one email address.
Without an index, Oracle has no choice. It reads every row, from the first to the last, and checks each email.
The plan calls this TABLE ACCESS FULL.
So we create an index on the email column.
Oracle builds a B-tree: the emails, sorted, in leaf blocks, with a few levels of guide keys above them.
To find our email, it starts at the root, follows one branch, and reaches the right leaf.
The leaf stores the row I D, the exact address of the row in the table. A few steps down the tree, instead of fifty thousand rows.
Explain plan shows how Oracle will run a query.
Before the index: TABLE ACCESS FULL, every row of customer.
After it: an INDEX RANGE SCAN finds the row I D, then TABLE ACCESS BY INDEX row I D fetches just that row.
The result is exactly the same. And remember: every primary key and UNIQUE constraint gets an index automatically.
An index can cover several columns. This one sorts customers by city, then by signup date, like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name.
It finds Madrid from twenty twenty-three quickly, and Madrid on its own too.
But a date on its own is spread across every city, so the index cannot go straight to it. That is the leftmost prefix rule.
Indexes are not free. Every insert, update or delete must also change each index of the table.
They also take disk space. So index the columns your queries filter, join or sort by, not every column.
One more trap. Wrap the column in a function, like lower of email, and the index on email can no longer be used.
The index is sorted by email, not by lower of email, so Oracle scans the table again.
The fix: a function-based index on exactly that expression.
Practise it in the SQL section of the course site.
